title: How to ask
description: Why a precise request gets a precise answer, and how to phrase things to get what you need.

steps.text: It often feels like the model “didn't get it.” But usually it isn't the model, it's the request: the vaguer you ask, the more room it has to answer off target. The precision of the question sets the precision of the answer.

Imagine asking a stranger for advice without giving any context or goal. They'd say something generic. It's the same with a model: “write a text” can be understood a hundred ways, and almost none of them is the one you meant.

steps.question: You write: “write a text about coffee.” What might the model decide you meant?
steps.answer: A social media post. Or a three-page article. Or a product-card description. Or a poem. Or a science note on caffeine. Every one of these is a correct answer to your request. Yours was just one of them.

steps.caption: A vague request fans out into dozens of answers; a precise one leads to one
Add details to the request: gray in the answer is what the model had to guess

steps.text: The first rule is specifics. Say exactly what you need, for whom and why. Not “tell me about sports” but “explain to a beginner in 5 sentences why warming up before a run matters.”

parts.note: a topic with no limits — the answer will read like an encyclopedia

parts.text: explain to a beginner why warming up before a run matters
parts.note: it's clear both what the topic is and who it's for

steps.text: The second is to set the format. Want a list, a table, a short paragraph, a simpler tone? Say so directly. A model readily adapts to a format, but only if you name it.

parts.text: what to take on a hike
parts.note: you'll get three paragraphs of solid text

parts.text: what to take on a two-day hike — as a list, bullet points, no explanations
parts.note: both the shape of the answer and its length are set

steps.text: Third: give me a role. “Answer like an experienced doctor” or “like a strict editor” — and I'll adjust style, depth and vocabulary to fit. A role is a quick way to tune the tone to the task.

steps.question: The question is the same: “is it okay to drink coffee on an empty stomach?” What changes if you assign the role of a doctor, and then of a barista?
steps.answer: The doctor will talk about acidity, the stomach and how long to wait after eating. The barista — about taste, strength and how the beans show their flavor without food. Same question, different role — and the answer looks in a completely different direction.

steps.text: And fourth: give an example or a sample, if you have one. A single example of “how it should look” works better than long explanations: the model picks up the style and repeats it.

parts.text: write a product description, shorter and livelier
parts.note: everyone understands “livelier” in their own way

parts.text: write a description in the same spirit: “A mug that will outlive your move. And the next one, too.”
parts.note: one sample sets the tone more precisely than three paragraphs of explanation

steps.situation: You need to write to your landlord: the kitchen faucet is dripping and you want it fixed.
steps.q: All three requests are long. Which will work best?
options: write a polite letter to my landlord: the kitchen faucet is dripping, please fix it, 5–6 sentences, calm tone
write a good letter to my landlord about the faucet, so he does everything properly there, you know what I mean, and fast
URGENT write a very stern letter to my landlord, threaten a lawsuit and fines, make him finally get moving
steps.explain: Length alone gives you nothing. The request “so he does everything properly there” has plenty of words but not a single specific: “good,” “properly” and “fast” can mean anything to the model. The letter threatening a lawsuit is specific but pulls away from your goal — you want a fixed faucet, not a fight. And the polite letter says what, to whom, in what tone and how long.

steps.text: And don't be afraid to clarify as you go. If the answer isn't right, don't start from scratch — adjust it: “shorter,” “add numbers,” “cut the fluff.” You're having a conversation, not taking a single shot.

parts.note: the model will pick the level

parts.text: why warming up before a run matters

steps.instruction: Each rule fixes its own trouble. Which goes with which?

pairs.def: an answer about “everything in general” instead of your topic
a wall of text where you needed a list
tone and depth that miss the task
right in meaning, but wrong in style

steps.template: A model can read “write a text” a hundred different ways, because the request has no ___.

steps.text: Practice. Think of a recent request whose answer came out “off target,” and rewrite it using the four rules: what exactly, in what format, from what role, following what sample. After the lesson, send me both versions in the chat — you'll see the difference right away.

In short. The precision of the question sets the precision of the answer. There are four levers: specifics (what, for whom, why), the format of the answer, the role of the one answering and a sample of “how it should look.” And if the answer isn't right, clarify as you go instead of starting over.

questions.q: Why does a vague request often get an answer that misses?
options: The model gets lazy with short questions and saves its effort on them
Fewer specifics leave the model more room to read it differently than you meant
The provider simply blocks requests that are too short to process
questions.explain: A vague request leaves the model many valid readings — and it will pick one that isn't yours.

questions.q: Which of these will improve the answer most?
options: Asking the same question several times in a row
Typing the whole request in capital letters
Stating the goal, the audience and the format
questions.explain: Specifics — the goal, who it's for, what form it takes — steer the model to the answer you want.

questions.q: Why give the model a role?
options: To tune tone, depth and vocabulary to the task
To make the answer arrive faster
So the model remembers you for good
questions.explain: A role is a quick way to turn the same question in the right direction: a doctor and a barista will answer differently.

questions.q: The answer came out wrong. What's the smarter move?
options: Delete everything and ask exactly the same thing again
Clarify within the chat: shorter, add numbers, change the tone
Decide the model just can't handle this at all
questions.explain: It's a conversation: a targeted tweak as you go is almost always faster than starting from zero.
